headline: McConnell is back in the Senate after three months away
summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the Senate Monday and cast his first vote since June, when a fall at home put him in the hospital. He was briefly unconscious and was treated for mild pneumonia. He says he is not quite back to 100% and is still in physical therapy. He retires in January after four decades in office.

cover_question.q: Why was he gone so long?

cover_answer: He fell at home, and getting better took months.
table_question: How long should a team hold your spot while you're out hurt?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A senator named Mitch McConnell fell at home this summer and went to the hospital. Today he went back to work for the first time. He was away about as long as summer break. He still does exercises to get stronger, and he's okay.
5-7.why: A fall and a comeback is a story a five-year-old already knows from the playground. The exercises make it ordinary.

8-12.script: Mitch McConnell fell at home in June and got pneumonia. His Senate seat sat empty for three months, so Republicans were a vote short and a farm bill got stuck. Today he came back and voted, like an injured starter cleared to play.
8-12.why: A fall, an empty seat, a stuck bill. Kids on a team know what one missing player costs.

13-17.script: How old is too old for a job other people depend on? Mitch McConnell, in the Senate since 1984, missed three months after a fall and said little for weeks. He came back today and voted. Who had a right to know, and when?
13-17.why: Teens already have opinions about old people in charge. Ask first.

5-7.a: He had a sickness called polio when he was little. It left his legs weak, so he falls more than most people. He's getting help so it happens less.

8-12.q: Why was he gone so long?
8-12.a: He fell at home, was knocked out for a bit, and got pneumonia in the hospital. He says he's still in physical therapy.

8-12.q: Who did his job while he was out?
8-12.a: Nobody can. A senator's vote is his alone, so his seat sat empty and a farm bill stalled in committee.

13-17.q: Should someone his age still be a senator?
13-17.a: Kentucky voters kept picking him for 40 years, and he retires in January. His absence raised that exact question in Washington.

13-17.q: Why didn't he tell people what was wrong?
13-17.a: He stayed quiet for weeks. Kentucky's governor publicly asked him to be transparent. He later said he'd been briefly unconscious and had pneumonia.
